title: Finding a leak with two heap snapshots
purpose: Find a leaked object by comparing two heap snapshots and reading its retainer path.
sequence_reason: Finding a leak is an ordered procedure: snapshot, repeat the action and its undo, snapshot again, compare, then follow the retainers. Each step needs the result of the step before it.
summary: In the Memory panel you take a heap snapshot, do a suspect action and undo it a few times, then take a second snapshot. The Comparison view lists objects that were added and are still alive. You select one, read its Retainers to see which reference keeps it alive, and clear that reference. A detached DOM node is the common case: it is removed from the page, but JavaScript still points to it.
explanation: Do the action and then undo it before the second snapshot. Anything still added after the undo is a leak candidate, and the Retainers section names the reference that keeps it alive.

learning_check.question: You remove a list from the page, but the second snapshot still shows a Detached ul. Where do you look to find what keeps it alive?
learning_check.answer: In the Retainers section of the selected object: it lists the objects that point to it, for example a JavaScript variable that still holds the list.

scenes.heading: Two snapshots find a leak
scenes.narration: A leak is memory that stays after you undo an action. Two heap snapshots show it.

visual.subtitle: Memory panel: snapshot, repeat, compare, follow the retainers

scenes.heading: The recipe in the Memory panel
scenes.narration: Take Snapshot 1. Do the suspect action, then undo it, a few times. Take Snapshot 2 and open the Comparison view.

items: Memory panel: Heap snapshot, Take snapshot
Do the suspect action, then undo it
Repeat the pair a few times

scenes.heading: What the Comparison view shows
scenes.narration: Each snapshot starts with a garbage collection, so only reachable objects stay. Objects added after the undo should be gone. If they are still there, something holds them.

right.label: Snapshot 2
items: Same @ object ID means the same object

visual.verdict: Added and still alive after the undo: a leak candidate.

scenes.heading: Follow the retainer path
scenes.narration: Select the added object. The Retainers section lists who points to it. Here a JavaScript variable still holds a list that the page removed, so it is a Detached ul.

path.label: Removed from the page, but JavaScript still points to it.

scenes.heading: Which object is worth fixing
scenes.narration: Shallow size is the memory the object holds itself. Retained size is what you free by deleting it. A small object can retain a lot.

right.label: Retained size
items: Memory freed by deleting the object
Includes what only it keeps alive

visual.verdict: Retained size tells you which object is worth fixing.

scenes.heading: Clear the reference, then check again
scenes.narration: Clear the variable that holds the list. Repeat the action and undo, take a new snapshot, and the Detached ul is gone.

items: Clear the variable that holds the list
Repeat the action and the undo
Take a new snapshot and compare

scenes.heading: When you do not know the action
scenes.narration: The Allocation Timeline records new memory over time. Each blue bar is a candidate leak. Zoom on a bar to see what was allocated then.
